clue.text: Runner — he has to round obstacle, at first

indicators.note: 'at first' tells us the word 'at' is placed at the front of the build

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: 'has to round' says the pronoun must go around the obstacle, enclosing it

parts.note: taken as written
a let is an obstacle or hindrance, as in 'without let or hindrance'

explanation.surface: A runner is told he must get round a hurdle at the start of a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has to round' puts the hindrance inside the pronoun, and 'at first' sends 'at' to the front. A let is the tennis term for an obstructed serve.
explanation.definitionFit: A track competitor who races is a typical sportsman of this kind.

clue.text: What queue is said to demand

definitions.text: What queue is said to demand

parts.words: What queue is said to demand
parts.note: queue sounds like Q, the abbreviation for question, and a question calls for a reply

explanation.surface: A line of people insists on something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'queue' looks like a line of people, but spoken it is the letter Q, short for question.
explanation.definitionFit: A question calls for a reply, the response it demands.

clue.text: End of speech, and most of another, in Hamlet

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, here from the word for a talk
'most of' says the final letter is dropped from the formal address

parts.note: another speech, that is an oration, a formal address

explanation.surface: The close of one speech and nearly all of another, in Shakespeare's play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'another' stands for another speech, a formal address, of which 'most of' keeps all but the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Horatio is Hamlet's loyal friend, a character in Shakespeare's tragedy.

clue.text: Such hardships we bear — constituents need Labour, nonetheless

indicators.note: the constituents of the words are their letters, which are mixed to form something new

parts.note: read as 'none the less': none is nought, O, which is taken away

explanation.surface: A political appeal: we put up with hardships, and voters need Labour all the same.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nonetheless' is split as 'none the less': none is zero, a ring-shaped letter, which is removed from the pool that 'constituents' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardships we can bear are ones that can be put up with or tolerated.

clue.text: Version of " Greenmantle "" in big print

indicators.note: a version of something is a reworked form, so the title's letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An edition of John Buchan's novel Greenmantle in large type.
explanation.walkthrough: Greenmantle is a John Buchan thriller; its letters rearrange, signalled by 'Version of'.
explanation.definitionFit: A photographic blow-up is a big print made from a smaller image.

clue.text: Potty ice-cream reforms EEC leader's wanting ?

indicators.note: 'reforms' says the letters of the frozen dessert are made into a new shape
'wanting' says a letter is lacking from that rearranged mix
the leader of a word is its first letter, here taken from the trading bloc's initials

explanation.surface: Someone goes crazy remaking ice cream for the European Economic Community, minus its head.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of ICE-CREAM, less the E that leads EEC, rearrange to give the answer; 'reforms' and 'wanting' signal both steps.
explanation.definitionFit: A potty is a pot, and pots are fired clay ware, so potty here means made of pottery.

clue.text: Skipping alternately across island

indicators.note: skipping every other letter of the next word leaves the alternate ones

explanation.surface: Someone skips back and forth across an island.
explanation.walkthrough: The second, fourth and sixth letters of 'across' give C, O, S.
explanation.definitionFit: Cos, also spelt Kos, is a Greek island in the Dodecanese.

clue.text: He wrote about a Dane's extremities

parts.note: RE is Latin for 'concerning', meaning about

indicators.note: the extremities of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: An author writes about a Dane's hands and feet.
explanation.walkthrough: The first and last letters of 'Dane's' (ignoring the 's) give D and E.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Reade was the Victorian novelist of The Cloister and the Hearth, a writer.

clue.text: After this drink, Henry was fired

definitions.text: After this drink, Henry was fired

parts.words: After this drink, Henry was fired
parts.note: the ...-Henry rifle of the Victorian army bore the name of a cocktail followed by Henry

explanation.surface: Henry lost his job after drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fired' looks like sacked but refers to shooting: the Martini-Henry was a British army rifle, the drink's name coming first.
explanation.definitionFit: This gin and vermouth cocktail shares its name with the Swiss designer of a rifle action.

clue.text: Such twopenny wares were far from plain

definitions.text: Such twopenny wares were far from plain

parts.words: Such twopenny wares were far from plain
parts.note: toy-theatre sheets were sold 'penny plain, twopence' for the painted version

explanation.surface: Cheap goods that were anything but simple.
explanation.walkthrough: Victorian toy-theatre sheets were sold 'penny plain, twopence coloured': the dearer ones were painted.
explanation.definitionFit: The twopenny sheets were tinted with paint, the opposite of plain.

clue.text: Steerforth's opening with schoolmate in brackets

indicators.note: the opening of a name is its first letter, taken from the Dickens character

parts.note: Tommy Traddles is David Copperfield's schoolmate at Salem House, as Steerforth is

explanation.surface: A Dickensian scene with Steerforth starting something alongside an old school friend.
explanation.walkthrough: Both Steerforth and Traddles are boys at David Copperfield's school in Dickens's novel. 'brackets' is a verb: to span or sit astride.
explanation.definitionFit: To bracket something is to span it from both sides, just as sitting astride does.

clue.text: March-past makes this fool's day

parts.note: the month that comes once March is past opens with the day of pranks on the first

explanation.surface: A military parade turns into a day for playing the fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'March-past' looks like a parade of soldiers, but read it as the time after the month of March.
explanation.definitionFit: The month after March begins with a day of practical jokes, its first day.

clue.text: Samson's paradoxical source of meat

parts.note: Samson's riddle in Judges: 'Out of the devourer came forth food', honey found in a lion's carcass

explanation.surface: A biblical puzzle about where a strongman got his food.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Book of Judges Samson sets the riddle 'Out of the eater came forth meat', meaning honey from a bees' nest in a dead lion.
explanation.definitionFit: In the riddle the consumer, the lion, is paradoxically where the food comes from.

clue.text: Cardinal well off with a place in France

parts.note: riche is the French word for rich or well off, the 'in France' covering both halves
lieu is the French word for a place

explanation.surface: A wealthy cardinal acquires a property in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in France' applies to both pieces: RICHE and LIEU are French words.
explanation.definitionFit: Cardinal Richelieu was the chief minister of Louis XIII of France, a churchman of that rank.

clue.text: Have they knights on? Church brasses do, possibly

indicators.note: 'possibly' says the words could be rearranged into another form

explanation.surface: A question about church brasses, which often show knights in armour.
explanation.walkthrough: Church brasses often depict knights, which is the surface; the knights in the definition are chess pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Chess knights stand on the squared boards the game is played on.

clue.text: Prepare to make 4? No, no!

definitions.meaning: to make a big print you double up the size of the photographic film image, 4 being the light ENLARGEMENT
saying no twice is two negatives in a row, which grammarians say cancel out

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense reads the phrase as an instruction: double (enlarge) the negative to make an enlargement, the answer to 4 down.
explanation.definitionFit: Enlarging a photograph means blowing up the film image; and a pair of noes is the grammatical fault of two denials.

clue.text: Outline a silly tax (as Shadow Cabinet might?)

parts.note: dumb is slang for silly or stupid
a rate is a local tax on property

explanation.surface: Sketching a foolish tax, as the opposition's Shadow Cabinet might.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket hints at the word's other sense, to overshadow, fitting a Shadow Cabinet.
explanation.definitionFit: To adumbrate is to sketch or give a faint indication of something.

clue.text: Old boys put right by medicine (not patent)

parts.note: OB is short for old boy, a former pupil, so the plural is OBS
to be cured is to be made well by treatment

explanation.surface: Former pupils are restored to health by medicine that is not a patent remedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'patent' here means obvious, not a patent medicine as the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Patent means plainly visible, so something hidden from view is its opposite.

clue.text: In London, a bishop's place on one of 13 ?

parts.note: George Berkeley, the philosopher, was Bishop of Cloyne
13 down is CHESSBOARDS, and each of those is made up of 64 squares

explanation.surface: A bishop in London moves to a spot on a chessboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In London' tells us where the place is: Berkeley Square is a square in Mayfair. A chess bishop also stands on a square, which adds to the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A London square is a public place, an open space surrounded by buildings.

clue.text: Azores wreck, for example, never raised

indicators.note: in a down clue 'raised' says the pieces are read upwards, backwards

explanation.surface: A shipwreck off the Azores that was never brought up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' turns the whole of EG plus NEVER upwards: REVEN then GE. The Revenge was Sir Richard Grenville's ship, lost off the Azores in 1591.
explanation.definitionFit: Grenville's galleon sank in a storm after its famous fight with a Spanish fleet off those islands.

clue.text: One at bridge is one of four in news

definitions.text: One at bridge is one of four in news

parts.words: One at bridge is one of four in news
parts.note: the four seats at a bridge table are North, East, West and South, whose initials spell news

explanation.surface: A bridge enthusiast makes the news as one of a group of four.
explanation.walkthrough: 'news' is N, E, W, S, the four compass seats at a card table.
explanation.definitionFit: Each of the four seated participants in a game of bridge sits at a compass point.

clue.text: Artist's firm about a drink — opposed to alcohol

definitions.note: the 's is read as 'is', so the clue says the artist is what the wordplay builds

indicators.note: 'about' says the company abbreviation goes around the other pieces

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm
a drink of beer is 'an ale', the article changing before the vowel
TT stands for teetotal, someone who refuses alcohol

explanation.surface: A painter's company is wrapped around a drink yet campaigns against alcohol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a drink' gives the article changed to suit the beer, not just the beer; 'about' wraps the company around that and the teetotal sign.
explanation.definitionFit: Canaletto was the eighteenth-century Venetian painter of city views.

clue.text: Chicken out of vote splitting left and right?

indicators.note: 'splitting' says the vote divides the pair of side abbreviations by going between them

parts.note: aye is a vote in favour

explanation.surface: A coward ducks out of a vote that divides the political left and right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chicken' looks like a coward, but it means a hen kept for eggs.
explanation.definitionFit: A hen kept for eggs is a laying bird.

clue.text: Being level? It's not when the fire goes out

indicators.note: 'goes out' says the word for a fire leaves the phrase before it

parts.note: an ingle is a fire on a domestic hearth, as in inglenook

explanation.surface: A question of whether something is flat, answered with a remark about a fire dying.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking INGLE out of BEING LEVEL leaves B, E and VEL. 'It's not' defines it: a sloped edge is the opposite of level.
explanation.definitionFit: A bevel is a slanted edge, so it is precisely not flat.

clue.text: Head of Harrow's plan for such school posts

definitions.text: Head of Harrow's plan for such school posts

parts.words: Head of Harrow's plan for such school posts
parts.note: the first letter of Harrow is H, and H is the outline of the goalposts in a game named after a school

explanation.surface: Harrow's headmaster has a scheme for staff jobs at another school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of Harrow' looks like the headmaster but means the letter H; 'plan' means outline, and the posts are goalposts shaped like H.
explanation.definitionFit: The game named after the Warwickshire public school uses H-shaped goalposts.

clue.text: Reason for better profits, no doubt ?

definitions.meaning: a 'better' is someone who bets, and a sure thing is what makes such a gambler win
a state of being completely sure

explanation.walkthrough: 'better' is not the comparative but a person who places bets.
explanation.definitionFit: A racing dead cert brings a punter winnings, and the word also means complete conviction.

clue.text: Hilton's master omits postscript in letter from Greece

indicators.note: 'omits' says the abbreviation for a postscript is left out

parts.note: Mr Chips is the schoolmaster in James Hilton's novel Goodbye, Mr Chips

explanation.surface: A schoolmaster leaves off the postscript of a letter sent from Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'letter' looks like correspondence, but it is a character of the Greek alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Chi is the twenty-second character of the Greek alphabet.

clue.text: Coins whose initial significance has gone

definitions.text: Coins whose initial significance has gone

parts.words: Coins whose initial significance has gone
parts.note: in old British money the d for pennies stood for these Roman coins, and decimalisation retired that letter

explanation.surface: Old coins that have lost their original value.
explanation.walkthrough: Before 1971 British money was pounds, shillings and pence, written £sd, where d stood for the Roman denarius. The initial d lost its meaning when decimal pence came in.
explanation.definitionFit: These were Roman silver coins, whose initial letter served for the British penny.

clue.text: Himalayan type less deadly when beheaded

definitions.text: Himalayan type less deadly when beheaded

parts.words: Himalayan type less deadly when beheaded
parts.note: Kipling's poem: the Himalayan peasant meets the male in his pride, but the female rends him; drop the first letter and the male remains

explanation.surface: A Himalayan creature becomes less dangerous once its head is cut off.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's 'The Female of the Species' opens with a Himalayan peasant meeting a he-bear and then the deadlier she-bear. Cut off the S and the female becomes the less deadly male.
explanation.definitionFit: A female bear of the Himalayas is the deadlier sex in Kipling's poem.
